title: the father runs
hookLine: the father runs — old men didn't run

cards: A grown son is walking up a dusty road toward the house he grew up in. He left badly. He took money that wasn't really his yet, and it's gone.
Now he's broke, and he's practicing a speech in his head, the way you might rehearse a hard phone call. He isn't hoping to be forgiven. He's hoping to be hired.
And while he's still far off, before he can say a word, he sees his father, an old man, running toward him.

teach.b: It's in Luke's Gospel, and it's usually called the Prodigal Son. Prodigal isn't in the story. It's an old word for wasteful, and the name came later.
A man has two sons. The younger asks for his share of the inheritance now, while his father is still alive; some readers hear in that: I wish you were already gone. The father gives it to him.
The son goes off to a far country and spends every coin.

Then a famine hits, and he ends up feeding pigs, hungry enough to envy what they eat. Then, in the old English, "when he came to himself," he rehearses his speech: I've sinned; make me one of your hired workers.

"But when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran, and fell on his neck, and kissed him." Some scholars of the period say a dignified older man didn't run in public.

The text only says he ran. Had compassion is the same Greek word Luke uses for yesterday's Samaritan: his gut turned over. The son starts the speech, and the father never lets him reach the part about being a servant.
He calls for the best robe, a ring, shoes and a feast. "For this my son was dead, and is alive again; he was lost, and is found."
But the older brother, who stayed and worked, hears the party and won't go in.

teach.h: HE WAS LOST, AND IS FOUND.
teach.b: The father goes out to him too, and pleads. The story ends there. We never find out if he goes in.

how: Christians read the Prodigal Son as a picture of God's welcome to anyone who returns. The Orthodox calendar names a Sunday before Lent after it, and Catholic and Orthodox teaching often connects it with confession and repentance.

games.q: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
p: asked for his share, and spent it
ran, and fell on his neck
heard the party and wouldn't go in

s: the word prodigal appears in the story itself
it doesn't. prodigal means wasteful, and the name was given to the story later.
the story ends with the older brother joining the feast
it ends with the father pleading with him outside. we never find out if he goes in.
the father's "had compassion" is the same Greek word Luke uses for the Samaritan
it means his gut turned over. Luke uses it in both stories.

games.q: you're the father. your younger son, who took his inheritance and wasted it, appears far down the road. he hasn't said a word yet. what do you do?
o: wait at the door to hear his apology.
run to him, and throw your arms around him.
send a servant to find out what he wants.
games.why: "when he was yet a great way off, his father saw him, and had compassion, and ran." a dignified old man running in public, before a word of the speech.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let a breath out. Think of a place, or a person, you've drifted from.
Maybe you left badly. Maybe it just faded. Picture the road back.
Now picture them seeing you from far off and coming toward you before you've said anything. Stay with that picture. If you pray, you can hold the father's words: he was lost, and is found.
If you don't, just let the picture be.

wordCard.voice: The Prodigal Son. The one who wasted everything, and the father who ran to meet him anyway. Thirteenth word.

orig.note: Greek. he had compassion; literally, his gut was moved. Luke uses it for the Samaritan (10:33) and for the running father (15:20).

carryVoice: Your line: you can come home. Christians have long heard the father as a picture of God: running to the one who left, walking out to the one who stayed. Day thirteen.
